title: One Mountain, Many Names
logline: Pilgrims of different faiths climb through the night to the same summit. Each calls it by a different name, and at dawn they all stand in front of the same stone, wind and light.

object.note: Object 1 (identity not chosen) could enter only if something ordinary genuinely passes to Chathura on the night climb or at the summit, for example something offered by a pilgrim. Never staged.

thread_out.thread: The dawn reached at the summit carries into the next film's question: when does 'morning' actually begin, and who decides it?

requirements: A single place genuinely named differently by different communities
Night and dawn access; safe filming on steps
Pilgrims willing to speak about the names they use

suggestions.name: Sri Pada / Adam's Peak (Samanalakanda, Sivanolipatha Malai)
suggestions.why: One mountain held sacred by Buddhist, Hindu, Muslim and Christian pilgrims, each with its own name and story.
suggestions.season_notes: Pilgrim season, roughly Unduvap Poya (Dec) to Vesak (May)
suggestions.access_notes: Crowded on poya weekends; Hatton (Nallathanni) and Ratnapura (Palabaddala) routes
suggestions.verify: Access, permissions and current conditions are unverified.

lesson.in_simple_terms: People can call the same mountain by many different names, and each name is useful to the people who use it. But a name is something we agree on; underneath all the names, every climber meets the same cold, wind and light.
lesson.in_simple_terms_si: එක කන්දකට නම් බොහොමයක් තිබුණත් ඒ නම් අප එකඟ වූ සම්මුති පමණක් වන අතර, ඒ නම්වලට යටින් හැමෝම විඳින්නේ එකම සීතලත් සුළඟත් එළියත්ය.
lesson.the_teaching: The Abhidhamma texts separate a name (a name-concept, nāma-paññatti) from the thing it calls to mind, and both from the ultimate realities (paramattha) that are actually present. A mountain is a 'collective' concept: a whole the mind takes up, which is not ultimately there as a separate thing. One text notes that the sound of a word is real, while the name it carries is a concept that lives in the hearer's understanding. The texts also say the Buddha deliberately taught in everyday names such as 'mountain' and 'river' so that people could understand easily, so conventional speech is not treated as a mistake.
lesson.how_the_film_shows_it: The film lets the viewer hear the mountain called by different names, in chants and greetings in several languages, while the camera stays on what the climbers share: breath in cold air, hands on railings, lamps along the steps. At dawn the talk falls away and for a moment there is only light, wind and stone in front of everyone. No one is told their name is wrong; the viewer simply notices that all the names were pointing at the same place.

key_terms.en: name-concept: the name that conveys a thing
conventional teaching: teaching in everyday names

lesson.caution: This does not mean any of the names is wrong or that the mountain is unreal; the texts treat everyday names as a valid way of speaking and keep what is actually there fully real.
lesson.builds_on: As the first film of the series, it opens the journey with the simplest step: noticing that a name and the thing it names are not the same.
lesson.evidence_class: editorial interpretation grounded in cited source teaching
